Abstract 41

Background 42

Clinical data analysis typically requires statistical programming skills, whereas 43

cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) agents risk exposing sensitive patient records. 44

We developed and functionally validated a privacy-preserving, zero-code 45

conversational statistical analysis framework that translates natural-language clinical 46

research requests into executable R workflows while strictly retaining raw patient data 47

within local computing environments. 48

Methods 49

Orchestrated by the n8n engine, the system integrates the DeepSeek-Reasoner model 50

with a Pinecone vector database for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), 51

grounding statistical selection in curated biostatistical guidance and R templates. Core 52

functionalities include data schema perception, interactive data cleaning, requirements 53

refinement, and local R code execution via a controlled command-line interface. 54

System performance was evaluated by replicating a published prognostic model study 55

on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). 56

Findings 57

All core analytical workflows — including data cleaning, multivariable Cox 58

proportional hazards modeling, model diagnostics, and publication-ready tables and 59

figures (e.g., baseline characteristics, Schoenfeld residuals, receiver operating 60

characteristic curves, and forest plots) — were executed solely through 61

natural-language dialogues without manual coding. The external large language 62

model actively clarified analytical prompts while receiving zero row-level patient 63

data. 64

Interpretation 65

Decoupling remote cloud reasoning from local code execution lowers the technical 66

threshold for clinicians conducting data-driven research while safeguarding data 67

privacy. This architecture provides a practical, scalable, and reproducible framework 68

for converting natural-language clinical questions into executable statistical 69

Research in context 78

Evidence before this study 79

We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore for 80

peer-reviewed research articles published from database inception up to 1 February 81

2026, using search terms including ("large language models" OR "agentic AI" OR 82

"conversational AI") AND ("clinical data analysis" OR "biostatistics" OR "R 83

execution") AND ("privacy-preserving" OR "local computation" OR 84

"retrieval-augmented generation"). No language restrictions were applied. Existing 85

clinical data analysis tools present a fundamental trade-off between analytical 86

flexibility and ease of use. While programming languages like R and Python offer 87

high flexibility and transparency, they require substantial statistical coding expertise. 88

Conversely, low-code or visual workflow platforms (e.g., KNIME, LinkR) reduce 89

coding demands but are constrained by pre-implemented, rigid analytical modules. 90

General-purpose AI coding agents (e.g., OpenAI Codex, Claude Code) enable 91

natural-language interaction but lack domain-grounded biostatistical frameworks to 92

ensure methodologically sound model specification and assumption evaluation. 93

Crucially, transmitting row-level patient data to external cloud-hosted LLM endpoints 94

poses severe data privacy, cybersecurity, and regulatory risks (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR). 95

To date, zero-code systems that effectively decouple cloud-based LLM reasoning 96

from local execution of raw patient data, while incorporating domain-specific 97

biostatistical knowledge grounding, remain scarce. 98

99

Added value of this study 100

To our knowledge, this study presents a novel, human-supervised, 101

privacy-preserving zero-code conversational statistical analysis system that 102

architecturally separates external LLM-assisted reasoning from local patient-level 103

data processing. Utilizing n8n as an orchestration platform, local R execution, and 104

Pinecone-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in curated 105

biostatistical guidance and R package documentation, the system translates 106

Incorporating a human-in-the-loop requirement refinement mechanism ensures that 108

investigators retain full control over judgment-dependent decisions, such as 109

missing-data handling and variable selection. We functionally validated the system by 110

fully reproducing a published prognostic model study for metabolic 111

117

Implications of all the available evidence 118

Our findings demonstrate that combining external agentic AI reasoning with local, 119

knowledge-grounded execution provides a safe, transparent, and cost-effective 120

solution for democratizing clinical data analysis. This architecture offers a scalable 121

and privacy-compliant blueprint for healthcare institutions seeking to empower 122

clinicians with advanced data analytics while strictly adhering to patient data 123

protection regulations. Future research should prioritize implementing closed-loop 124

automated error correction, semi-automated knowledge base curation, and formal 125

multi-center usability and statistical validity evaluations with clinical end-users. 126

Introduction 127

In contemporary medical research, data-driven decision-making and discovery have 128

become central forces driving progress in the field. The widespread adoption of 129

electronic health records (EHRs) has generated large volumes of structured clinical 130

data that can support observational research, prognostic modelling, and healthcare 131

quality improvement.1,2 However, the abundance of data resources has not been 132

equivalently translated into efficient research output. Despite increasing data 133

availability, many healthcare institutions continue to face challenges in converting 134

routinely collected clinical data into reproducible scientific evidence. This gap is 135

particularly evident in institutional and multicenter EHR databases, where data 136

acquisition often outpaces analytical capacity. Although the development of EHRs has 137

enabled the large-scale digital collection of numerous clinical indicators and 138

follow-up records, frontline clinicians and researchers continue to face substantial 139

difficulties in transforming these data into evidence-based medical insights.3,4 140

One major contributor to this gap is the disconnect between clinical expertise and 141

the technical skills required to perform modern statistical analyses. Many 142

clinician-investigators, who are experts in understanding the clinical implications of 143

data, lack formal training in statistical programming languages such as R or Python. 144

Consequently, translating clinical research questions into reproducible analytical 145

workflows often requires substantial programming support. This skill barrier not only 146

reduces research efficiency but also limits the depth of data-driven insights that can be 147

extracted from available datasets.5 148

To bridge this gap, both academia and industry have explored various approaches. 149

Traditional manual programming, while powerful, demands substantial time 150

investment for syntax learning and debugging, resulting in a steep learning curve. 151

Graphical user interface (GUI)-based statistical software such as SPSS, SAS 152

Enterprise Guide, and GraphPad Prism, reduces operational difficulty through 153

menu-driven interfaces but often provides limited flexibility for highly customized 154

analytical workflows, which may restrict complex or iterative analyses. Low-code or 155

The emergence of large language models (LLMs) for code generation has opened a 161

novel pathway, yet current implementations exhibit inherent limitations in medical 162

statistical tasks: (1) Limited awareness of local datasets: Stand-alone LLM interfaces 163

do not inherently maintain reliable awareness of local dataset schemas, variable 164

definitions, or analytical state. The code they generate often contains "hallucinations" 165

including fabrication of column names, inappropriate package selection, and 166

generation of non-executable code. (2) Inability to execute and verify automatically: 167

Users must manually copy, paste, execute, and debug generated code, breaking 168

workflow continuity. (3) Contextual discontinuity: In multi-step complex analyses, 169

LLMs struggle to maintain consistent context across multiple conversation turns. 170

(4) Privacy and governance concerns: Many high-performance LLM services rely on 171

cloud-based inference, raising governance concerns when patient-level information is 172

transmitted outside institutional environments. This conflicts with the stringent data 173

privacy protection requirements in medical research.9-10 (5) Limited reproducibility of 174

generated analytical workflows: Variability in prompt interpretation and code 175

generation may produce inconsistent analytical workflows across repeated sessions.11 176

Recently, several cutting-edge architectures have attempted to address these 177

challenges. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic, establishes 178

a standardized open interface for connecting LLMs with local databases;12 however, 179

MCP primarily facilitates communication between models and external tools and does 180

not itself ensure methodological validity, statistical appropriateness, or analytical 181

reproducibility. Similarly, modular instruction architectures such as Skill.md can 182

improve performance on specific tasks but lack systematic design for the complex, 183

long-chain workflow from data cleaning to hypothesis testing.13 184

Given these limitations, a privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted 185

lack dedicated programming or statistical expertise, while ensuring patient data 187

privacy through fully localized operation, could substantially accelerate clinical 188

research productivity, improve analytical reproducibility, and facilitate broader 189

participation in data-driven healthcare innovation. Such a system should preserve 190

human oversight of study design, variable selection, missing-data management, and 191

model interpretation rather than fully automating analytical decision-making. This 192

potential is especially meaningful in resource-limited environments where access to 193

dedicated statistical expertise is constrained. Critically, such a system should be 194

positioned as an intelligent collaborator that augments rather than replaces 195

professional statisticians. 196

The emergence of agentic AI offers a promising architectural paradigm to realize 197

this vision, yet its reliability and applicability in highly specialized and rigorous 198

medical research scenarios require further empirical validation.14 199

In this study, we aimed to develop and validate a human-supervised conversational 200

statistical analysis system that combines agentic workflow orchestration, 201

retrieval-augmented generation, and local R execution. The resulting analytical 202

system will empower clinicians to independently perform routine analytical tasks. 203

Methods 204

Environment Configuration and Deployment 205

The analysis environment was deployed on a local workstation using Node.js and 206

n8n (v2.14.2) as the workflow orchestration engine and R (v4.7.3) as the statistical 207

computing backend. wenty-three preinstalled R packages supporting data 208

manipulation, statistical modelling, survival analysis, machine learning, and 209

visualization (e.g., tidyverse, survival, glmnet, pROC, ggplot2) was used. n8n 210

orchestrates workflow execution and data exchange, whereas R scripts are executed 211

locally through the Rscript interface to perform statistical analyses and generate 212

graphical outputs. Communication between n8n and R occurs through predefined 213

local file paths and command-line invocation, ensuring that all patient-level data 214

processing and statistical computation remain local (Figure 1). 215

216

Data Privacy and Local Processing 217

The system was designed to prevent transmission of row-level patient records to 218

external LLM services. Metadata transmitted to the LLM included variable names, 219

inferred data types, missingness summaries, and high-level distribution characteristics. 220

Complete patient-level records remained within the local workstation throughout the 221

analytical workflow. The LLM is accessed via API only with this anonymized 222

structural information, and all generated R code was executed locally within the R 223

environment. This architecture minimizes external exposure of patient-level clinical 224

data while allowing LLM-assisted code generation and workflow orchestration. 225

226

System Architecture Overview 227

To bridge the gap between natural-language clinical queries and the execution of 228

reproducible statistical workflows without exposing sensitive patient records to 229

external servers, the proposed system implements a four-tier Systematic Layered 230

Architecture (Figure 2). This architecture segregates the user experience, logic 231

orchestration, AI reasoning, and data computation into independent operational 232

Layer 1: Interface & Interaction. This outermost layer establishes a 234

Layer 2: Workflow Orchestration. Serving as the central controller of the system, 238

this layer managed sequential and conditional execution logic using localized 239

Layer 3: Cognitive Reasoning & RAG Retrieval. This layer governs requirement 244

multi-step dialogues. To systematically mitigate model hallucinations, a RAG 247

within verified biostatistical knowledge bases and standardized R coding 249

specifications. 250

Layer 4: Local Execution & Data. Acting as the ultimate security perimeter for 251

patient privacy, this foundational layer enforces absolute local data isolation. The 252

synthesized statistical scripts are dispatched to a sandboxed local environment where 253

all patient-level data transformations, mathematical modeling, and figure generation 254

are executed entirely offline against the local storage, guaranteeing that raw row-level 255

patient data never leave the investigator's local infrastructure. 256

Core Analysis Pipeline 258

The analytical process is implemented as two interacting workflows (Figure 3). 259

Human–AI Interaction Loop Workflow 1 – Local Data Profiling and Preprocessing: 260

After a researcher uploads a CSV file, a Code node extracts the table structure and 261

identifies potentially extreme observations using both interquartile range (IQR)-based 262

275

Implementation of the Core Algorithm 276

The system automates the traditional epidemiological analysis workflow (data 277

perception, data cleaning, requirement refinement, and code execution) through four 278

integrated components. 279

Intelligent Data Perception and Interactive Data Cleaning 280

Researchers can launch this workflow by specifying the variables to be included in 281

the analysis (i.e., target variables) via natural language. The system then automatically 282

loads the CSV file and scans the dataset. Relying on predefined clinical terminology 283

dictionaries and heuristic classification rules, it automatically infers the storage type 284

of each variable (continuous, binary, categorical, ordinal, date/time, or identifier) and 285

determines its applicable analytical role (continuous, categorical, ordinal, or 286

identifier). Meanwhile, the system identifies all missing values based on the missing 287

value pattern library and processes them following standard schemes. Our system 288

provides two predefined missing-data management options for investigator selection: 289

1. Perform simple imputation for variables with less than 15% missing data (median 290

imputation for continuous variables, mode imputation for categorical variables); 2. 291

delete all cases with missing values for variables with a missing rate of 15% or higher. 292

AI-Assisted Requirement Refinement 305

The researcher expresses analytical intent in natural language (e.g., “compare liver 306

function indicators between the survival group and the death group”). The AI Agent 307

compares the analytical request against the available data dictionary and proposes 308

candidate analytical approaches, retrieves relevant methodological guidance and 309

diagnostic considerations from the Pinecone knowledge base. It then returns 310

supplementary recommendations, such as suggesting non-parametric tests when the 311

data deviate from normality. Once the researcher confirms or adjusts the suggestions, 312

the investigator-confirmed structured analytical plan is submitted through the 313

dialogue interface, and the system proceeds to generate the corresponding code. 314

Intelligent Code Generation and Execution 315

After the analytical plan is confirmed, a dedicated AI Agent generates an 316

executable R analysis script. The system prompt strictly constrains the agent to use 317

fixed local file paths, automatically perform variable type conversions (e.g., 318

converting categorical variables to factors), and select appropriate statistical tests and 319

visualization functions. The generated code is cleaned of Markdown formatting and 320

executed via the Rscript command in the local R environment. All outputs (tables and 321

figures) are saved to a designated local directory, while maintaining local execution of 322

Construction of the Clinical Research and Biostatistics Knowledge Base 324

The Pinecone vector database stores five categories of domain knowledge: R 325

programming standards, publication-style figure templates, biostatistical methodology 326

guidance, R package recommendations, and interactive requirement templates. During 327

both requirement refinement and code generation, the AI Agent is mandated to query 328

this knowledge base. The query text is embedded into a vector, and the most relevant 329

knowledge snippets are retrieved by cosine similarity and injected into the generation 330

context. This RAG design mitigates the “hallucination” problem of large language 331

models in medical statistical tasks at two levels. First, the verified statistical strategies 332

and code templates in the knowledge base provide curated reference material 333

reviewed for methodological and coding relevance. This substantially reduces the 334

probability of fabricating nonexistent R functions or erroneously selecting statistical 335

methods due to a lack of professional knowledge. Second, when a complex analytical 336

task is detected (e.g., drawing a Kaplan-Meier curve or building a Cox regression 337

model), the system proactively retrieves parameter templates from the knowledge 338

base and guides the researcher with structured questions to supply key parameters. 339

This step reduces the likelihood of unsupported assumptions when analytical 340

information is incomplete. Although RAG cannot eliminate all coding or 341

methodological errors, it constrains code generation using curated statistical resources 342

and standardized analytical templates. 343

Results 360

System implementation and workflow completion 361

The final system comprised two interconnected workflows: (1) Automated Data 362

Preprocessing (Figure S1a, b), and (2) Automated Statistical Analysis & Reporting 363

(Figure S1c). Functional validation was conducted by reproducing the principal 364

analyses of a published metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease 365

(MASLD) prognostic model study.15 The investigator initiated and confirmed 366

analytical decisions through natural-language interaction without manually writing or 367

executing any R code. A representative dialogue sequence is shown in Figure 4; 368

complete prompts, responses, generated code, and output files are provided in 369

Supplementary Appendix E. 370

371

Replication of the published analysis 372

The system performed all prespecified analytical steps: (i) Kaplan – Meier 373

estimation, (ii) descriptive analyses with univariable Cox regression, (iii) 374

multivariable Cox regression and model performance evaluation, and (iv) ROC curve 375

generation. The resulting tables, Kaplan–Meier curves, and forest plots are provided 376

in the Supplementary Material (Tables S1–S4 and Figure S2–S3); and the ROC curve 377

is displayed in Figure 2 of the main text. Three tasks were executed successfully on 378

the first attempt, whereas the remaining task required an iterative workflow reuse. 379

Specifically, the initially refined analysis commands were re-submitted to further 380

normative optimization, thereby generating a more comprehensive and accurate 381

analytical directive that ultimately enabled the AI agent to produce rigorous 382

executable code.The final model, determined by stepwise regression, retained 13 383

variables: age, body mass index, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, 384

diastolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, fasting blood glucose, aspartate 385

aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, gamma- glutamyl transferase, platelet 386

count, total bilirubin, and creatinine. This set differs slightly from that of the original 387

study, which included sex and alkaline phosphatase instead of body mass index and 388

394

Analytical fidelity 395

The reproduced effect estimates were consistent with those reported in the 396

reference study. The absolute relative differences in hazard ratios ranged from 0.003 397

to 0.183, and the difference in time-dependent AUCs remained below 0.034.15 The 398

5-year AUC from our system was 0.786, compared with 0.764 in the original study. 399

400

Processing time and reproducibility 401

The complete workflow, from data ingestion to final output generation, required 402

approximately 3 hours. Importantly, re-execution of the saved R scripts in the same 403

software environment produced identical numerical outputs. No manual modification 404

of the final R scripts was required. 405

406

Data Privacy and Security 407

All patient- level data processing and statistical computation were performed within 408

the local workstation, and no data were transmitted to external servers. To further 409

protect participant privacy, the raw data were processed through a dedicated 410

structure- extraction node that generated column-level summaries (e.g., data types, 411

missing rates, distributional characteristics) without exposing any complete patient 412

records. This ensured that the LLM, which handled only the aggregated structural 413

metadata, could not access sensitive patient information (Figure S4). 414

Discussion 415

In this proof-of-concept study, we developed and functionally validated a 416

human-supervised, zero-code conversational statistical analysis system that combines 417

agentic workflow orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and local R 418

execution. Using natural-language interaction, the system completed the prespecified 419

analytical workflow of a published study, including data-quality assessment, survival 420

analysis, Cox regression, model diagnostics, and generation of publication-formatted 421

tables and figures. Patient-level data processing and statistical computation remained 422

within the local workstation, while the external LLM was restricted to analytical 423

requirement refinement and R code generation using predefined dataset metadata and 424

retrieved statistical guidance. The principal contribution of this system is therefore not 425

simply automated code generation, but the architectural separation of external 426

LLM-assisted reasoning from local patient-level computation within an 427

investigator-supervised and auditable workflow. 428

429

Comparison with Existing Clinical Data Analysis Approaches 430

Existing approaches to clinical data analysis often involve a trade-off between 431

analytical flexibility and ease of use. Programming environments such as R and 432

Python provide extensive flexibility and transparency but require proficiency in 433

statistical coding. In contrast, graphical and low-code platforms reduce programming 434

demands but generally require investigators to select appropriate methods, configure 435

analytical parameters, and interpret statistical assumptions. 436

Visual workflow platforms such as KNIME and Galaxy enable users to construct 437

transparent and reusable analytical pipelines with limited manual coding. However, 438

investigators must still identify the appropriate analytical modules, specify parameters, 439

evaluate assumptions, and interpret the resulting outputs.16-19 Healthcare-oriented 440

low-code platforms such as LinkR further improve the accessibility of data 441

manipulation and statistical analysis. However, their functionality remains dependent 442

on the analytical modules and workflows implemented within the platform.7 443

General-purpose coding agents, including OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, permit 444

natural-language interaction with source code and can generate, execute, and revise 445

analytical scripts. However, these tools are primarily designed for general 446

software-engineering tasks and do not inherently provide a curated framework for 447

clinical epidemiologic study design, biostatistical method selection, or assessment of 448

model assumptions.20-23 Biomedical AI platforms such as Polly Co-Scientist provide 449

greater domain specialization but are designed to augment broader biomedical 450

research workflows rather than serve as a transparent, general-purpose system for 451

conversational clinical statistical analysis. In addition, workflows that transmit 452

patient-level data to externally hosted models require appropriate contractual, 453

regulatory, privacy, and cybersecurity safeguards. These considerations identify a 454

need for a knowledge-grounded conversational system that reduces the requirement 455

for manual programming while preserving investigator control, statistical 456

transparency, and local processing of patient-level data. 457

458

Architectural and Methodological Contributions 459

The proposed system addresses these gaps through the integration of conversational 460

requirement refinement, retrieval-grounded R code generation, local statistical 461

execution, and preservation of an auditable analytical record. First, the system allows 462

investigators to initiate and refine multistep analytical tasks through natural-language 463

interaction without using R code. It translates investigator-specified decisions 464

regarding data cleaning, variable selection, statistical modelling, model diagnostics, 465

and output formatting into executable R scripts and publication-formatted analytical 466

outputs. Second, the requirement-refinement process presents proposed analytical 467

specifications to the investigator for review and confirmation before code execution. 468

This human-in-the-loop design preserves investigator control over 469

judgment-dependent decisions, including missing-data management, outlier handling, 470

covariate selection, model specification, and interpretation of diagnostic findings. 471

Third, the architecture separates external LLM-assisted reasoning from local 472

patient-level computation. Row-level data transformations, statistical modelling, and 473

generation of final outputs are performed within the local workstation, whereas the 474

external LLM receives only the predefined metadata and aggregate information 475

required to refine the analytical request and generate R code. Fully local deployment 476

of an open-weight LLM represents an alternative approach that can avoid external 477

model inference. However, it may require substantial computing infrastructure, model 478

deployment expertise, maintenance, and local validation. Moreover, local hosting 479

addresses the location of data processing but does not itself prevent hallucination. 480

Fourth, the system combines a free self-hosted n8n Community Edition, the 481

open-source R statistical environment and R packages, locally hosted embedding 482

models, and usage-based external services for LLM inference and vector retrieval. 483

Although it is not entirely open-source or cost-free, this architecture avoids the 484

licensing costs of commercial statistical software. Furthermore, because the LLM API 485

is used exclusively for text generation (R code and natural language dialogue), the 486

per-analysis token cost is substantially lower than that of tools relying on multimodal 487

models or extensive cloud computation. These combined cost advantages make the 488

system particularly suitable for resource-limited settings, where dedicated statistical 489

expertise and commercial analytical tools are financially inaccessible. 490

A central design objective was to mitigate the risk of hallucinations (unsupported, 491

non-executable, or statistically inappropriate outputs) from LLMs. The system 492

addresses this risk through three complementary mechanisms. First, local schema 493

profiling provides the LLM with predefined information regarding variable names, 494

storage types, analytical roles, missingness, and distributional characteristics, 495

reducing reliance on assumed dataset structures. Second, retrieval-augmented 496

generation (RAG) grounds method selection and code construction in curated 497

biostatistical guidance, R package documentation, reporting recommendations, and 498

validated code and visualization templates. Third, all numerical analyses are delegated 499

to the R statistical environment, and the resulting scripts and outputs remain available 500

for investigator inspection, execution review, and reproduction. Together, these 501

mechanisms constrain the generation process and reduce the likelihood of fabricated 502

variables, nonexistent functions, and unsupported analytical assumptions. 503

Nevertheless, retrieval grounding does not independently validate the appropriateness 504

Finally, the system accelerates the translational cycle of clinical research by 507

compressing workflows that traditionally require days into hours. Preservation of the 508

final R scripts, data-processing decisions, package versions, and analytical outputs 509

supports transparency and computational reproducibility once the code has been 510

finalized. Regarding reproducibility, it should be distinguished at the code-execution 511

and LLM-generation levels. A frozen R script can reproduce identical numerical 512

results when executed with the same data, software versions, and random seeds. In 513

contrast, repeated LLM interactions may generate different analytical plans or code 514

because of model stochasticity, model updates, prompt variation, and differences in 515

retrieved knowledge. Reproducibility of the complete conversational workflow 516

therefore requires preservation of the model identifier, system and user prompts, 517

retrieved knowledge snippets, generated code, package versions, random seeds, and 518

execution logs. 519

Limitations and Future Directions 521

Several limitations of the current implementation warrant acknowledgment. The 522

non-deterministic nature of LLM code generation means that syntax errors or 523

suboptimal statistical choices may still occur. The current system captures execution 524

errors and terminates, but lacks an automated error-correction feedback loop, which is 525

an important direction for future development. Dependence on external LLM APIs 526

introduces vulnerability to network latency and service interruptions. The initial 527

construction and ongoing maintenance of the knowledge base require manual expert 528

curation; future work will explore semi-automated literature mining approaches to 529

reduce this burden. The system currently supports only structured tabular data and 530

does not yet extend to unstructured data types such as medical images or free-text 531

clinical notes. Furthermore, user input with high ambiguity or internal contradictions 532

may exceed the capacity of the current requirement clarification mechanism; a more 533

In conclusion, this proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of using a 538

human-supervised, retrieval-grounded conversational system to translate clinical 539

research questions into transparent R code while retaining patient-level computation 540

within a local environment. The architecture’s principal contribution is the separation 541

of external LLM-assisted reasoning from local statistical execution, combined with 542

investigator control and preservation of an auditable analytical record. Multidomain 543

validation, formal comparisons with existing analytical approaches, and prospective 544

usability, security, and statistical-validity evaluations are required before broader 545

institutional research deployment. 546
